In addition to following the outlined DHSC architecture framework, consider scalability and
sustainability when selecting digital solutions for the health supply chain. A key mandate of the
TWG should be oversight in this area.
Ð While upstream health supply chain levels such as the central warehouse use advanced systems to manage
inventory and distribution, it is important to have sufficient system coverage at the lowest supply chain
level to capture actual consumption. Health supply chains typically rely on inventory distribution data
from warehouses or data on inventory issues from pharmacies to determine consumption. However, actual
consumption should include what is dispensed to individuals, product expiries, wastages and inventory
shrinkage. Systems, especially at the last mile of the supply chain, should have the ability to track and capture
batch details and serial numbers, where available, as part of product expiries, wastages, inventory shrinkage

narrative.text: Fig 14, 'DHSC architecture framework'. Inside a frame labelled DIGITAL HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN ENTERPRISE: SHARED SERVICES (foundational components: facility, product and supplier registries), DATA SERVICES (analytics — supply chain reports, data warehouse; traceability — track and trace, product verification) and Digital ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). Below them, an INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. At the bottom, HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS (forecasting and planning, order, warehouse and cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing), beside EXTERNAL SYSTEMS (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Callouts explain each layer — for example, that OpenHIM is a useful reference for interoperability components, and SCISMM and TSS v2 for the supply chain systems.

The DHSC architecture — shared services, data services, digital ecosystems, an interoperability layer of enabling components, and external systems — with its health supply chain information systems divided by level. narrative.text: Fig 20, 'Benefits of cross-enterprise analytics services'. Along the bottom runs the physical supply chain: manufacturing, shipping, regulatory customs, central-warehouse receiving and inventory management, distribution, regional-warehouse replenishment, health-facility dispensing, and patients. Above it sit the planning processes: forecasting and planning; supplier and contract management; procurement; and order management. Dashed arrows carry 'Transactional data from systems relevant to the supply chain' up through the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER into DATA SERVICES — analytics: supply chain reports and a data warehouse. A callout lists the questions analytics services answer: optimizing inventory against consumption to minimize stockouts, whether planned supplies will arrive in time, forecast accuracy against actual consumption, on-time and in-full delivery, wastage and leakage, stock at risk of expiry and where to move it, where and how often stockouts occur, and supplier performance.

narrative.text: Fig 23, 'Cost components to determine the total cost of ownership'. A dashed loop labelled 'Total cost of ownership' encloses four groups of cost components. IMPLEMENT: sourcing (RFP, RFI, RFQ), software, hardware and infrastructure, design and development, integration and interoperability, testing and training, and deployment. SCALE: expansion of deployment, training, and hardware and infrastructure. OPERATE: software subscriptions, maintenance (personnel, software, hardware), ongoing training, and monitoring and evaluation. ONGOING: management, governance and overhead. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

narrative.text: Fig 24, 'Achieving track and trace capabilities through DHSC architecture components'. Along the bottom, the supply chain runs from regulator through central, regional and district warehouses to health facilities and patients. Each location's system — regulator systems, warehouse management, transportation management, inventory management, dispensing, and verification at the patient — exchanges data in both directions with the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER, as do the external systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Above the layer, DATA SERVICES hold analytics and traceability (track and trace, product verification). A callout lists the questions traceability services answer: where a batch is now, whether supply chain integrity was maintained, who had custody on a date, where a batch was dispensed, whether the product moved through known locations, whether there were anomalies, and whether the product is genuine. A legend defines traceability data as what (product, batch and serial number), when, where and why (the transaction type).

narrative.text: Fig 25, 'Illustrative example of a traceability service interface'. At the top is a mock screen, 'Track and trace results for product 001001123123', batch A1001234. It shows a timeline of five verified events with their location and timestamp: verified and received at the central warehouse (11 Mar 2023); shipped from the central warehouse (5 Apr); verified and received at health facility 001 (6 Apr); verified and dispensed there (10 Apr); and a final patient-side verification of serial number 202 with GPS coordinates (10 Apr, 16:14). Below, the flow that produces it: the manufacturer, central/regional warehouse and health facilities emit ship, receive and dispense events, and handheld verify scans are made along the way. All of these feed DATA SERVICES (analytics and traceability), which answer the screen's query for the product code, batch, its serial numbers 201 to 204 and the expiry date.
